headline: High-risk filesystem and tool-use overlap: OpenHands can write/browse/run tools while Dagster is a non-runnable orchestrator with no direct I/O, so prompt-injection and leakage are limited but capability conflict and cascading misuse…

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Dagster has no clipboard, filesystem, or MCP surfaces, so it cannot directly ingest OpenHands output by default. OpenHands can use MCP and browser/file tools, but the pair lacks a documented shared channel. The only plausible bridge is manual transfer or mounted files, which is not shown here, so prompt injection is limited.
conditions: IF a shared file or MCP channel is introduced between Dagster and OpenHands, then injected instructions can cross the boundary.
IF OpenHands output is manually copied into Dagster task definitions, then prompt injection becomes possible.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Disable any shared MCP server between them.
Avoid copy-pasting OpenHands outputs into Dagster configs.
Add a review step before Dagster consumes any OpenHands-generated text.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Dagster touches no files or secrets in its profile, while OpenHands reads and writes only files mounted into its runtime and sends data to a user-configured model provider. There is no documented shared workspace or sensitive data class overlap, so leakage is possible only if operators mount the same sensitive files into both.
conditions: IF the same mounted volume contains sensitive files for both agents, then OpenHands can read data Dagster does not touch.
IF OpenHands is configured with a third-party model provider and sensitive files are mounted, then those contents may leave the runtime.
mitigations: Mount only least-privilege files into OpenHands.
Keep Dagster and OpenHands on separate volumes.
Remove secrets from any shared runtime directory.
Use a local model provider for OpenHands when handling sensitive files.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands has broad write, shell, git, and network capabilities inside its runtime, while Dagster is non-runnable and has no write or network surfaces. If both are pointed at the same mounted directory or repo, OpenHands can mutate state that Dagster cannot coordinate or lock, creating destructive conflicts and inconsistent pipeline state.
conditions: IF both agents share the same mounted repository or workspace, then OpenHands can overwrite files Dagster expects to be stable.
IF Dagster schedules jobs against a repo that OpenHands is editing, then git and filesystem races can corrupt state.
mitigations: Use separate repositories or branches.
Mount the workspace read-only for Dagster.
Pause OpenHands before Dagster writes to shared paths.
Add file-locking around any shared mutable directory.
requires-engineering: implement orchestrator-level coordination locks.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Dagster is a data orchestrator and OpenHands is an agent loop with shell/browser/editor actions, so OpenHands outputs can plausibly become Dagster inputs if operators wire them together. Dagster does not verify those outputs by default, and OpenHands can generate or modify artifacts that Dagster later executes, making cascading mistakes realistic.
conditions: IF Dagster ingests OpenHands-generated configs, code, or task parameters without review, then errors can cascade.
IF OpenHands edits files that Dagster later executes, then a mistaken change can propagate downstream.
mitigations: Require human review of OpenHands outputs before Dagster consumes them.
Validate generated configs with schema checks.
Run Dagster in dry-run mode for new artifacts.
Separate generation and execution workspaces.

E_compliance.rationale: Dagster is open-source and shows no touched data classes, while OpenHands handles files in its runtime and model-provider API keys. The pair can create retention and residency mismatches if sensitive files are mounted into OpenHands and sent to a configured third-party provider, but the profiles do not show a specific regulated data class, so this is not higher.
conditions: IF regulated data is mounted into OpenHands and the configured model provider is outside the required residency boundary, then a compliance breach can occur.
IF Dagster-managed artifacts include retention-sensitive records and OpenHands writes them to its runtime, then retention policy mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Do not mount regulated data into OpenHands.
Use a provider with an approved residency boundary.
Set short retention on OpenHands runtime volumes.
Document which data classes may flow through each agent.
